_: Battle Map: The Battle of Tours (732). Narration by films/director/script.py; prepared by harness/shots/prep.py.

music.prompt: Instrumental early medieval score: low frame drum, bowed lyre, droning hurdy gurdy and a solemn male choir hum, with a hint of oud and darbuka for the Umayyad side. Starts quiet and suspenseful at a slow walking tempo, builds to a driving, pounding middle with repeated drum hits for the charges, drops to a hush for the night, then ends with a warm, slightly playful resolution.

prep.voice_brief: an upbeat, warm, playful, completely natural-sounding narrator for an animated history map for kids, with dry deadpan humour
prep.voice_instructions: Warm, upbeat, playful storyteller narrating an exciting animated history map for kids aged 8 to 14. Natural and conversational, like a favourite teacher who loves this story: real energy and a smile in the voice, a dry deadpan touch on the jokes, a little awe on the big moments. Never robotic, never a movie-trailer announcer. Brisk pace, natural pauses.

vo.text: In October 732, or 733 by some historians' count, an army mostly on foot packed together in France and simply refused to move. It worked better than anyone expected.
Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of Muslim Spain, led an Umayyad army north over the Pyrenees. He had already beaten Duke Odo of Aquitaine near Bordeaux.
Therefore Odo hurried to an old rival for help: Charles Martel, leader of the Franks.
The Umayyads were heading for Tours and its rich abbey. But Charles blocked the road somewhere between Poitiers and Tours. Nobody knows the exact spot.
His plan was simple. His men packed into a tight square and waited. The chroniclers say the two armies watched each other for about a week.
But soon the fast Umayyad cavalry charged, again and again, all day long. But the Franks did not break. One chronicler wrote that they stood like a wall, frozen together like ice.
But late in the day, Abd al-Rahman fell in the fighting. Therefore his army pulled back to its camp as night came.
At dawn the Franks lined up again, ready for round two. But the tents were empty. The army had slipped away south in the dark.
Charles later earned the nickname Martel, meaning the Hammer. Not bad for a man whose best move was standing perfectly still.
